shipped_rows.title_o: Does Economic Growth Improve the Human Lot? Some Empirical Evidence

blind_target.title: Feeding the illusion of growth and happiness: A reply to Hagerty and Veenhoven
blind_target.evidence_quote:
Richard Easterlin elegantly disputed these findings in a paper: Feeding the
      Illusion of Growth and Happiness: A Reply to Hagerty and Veenhoven, published in this
      journal (Easterlin 2005).
blind_target.outcome_quote:
All in all, it seems that people have become happier in the second half of the 20th century
    and that the gains in happiness have been greater in poor nations than in rich nations.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The extended national survey series contradict the closest target in the debate: Easterlin’s 2005 no-growth interpretation. The overall judgment is rising happiness despite measurement uncertainty.

luna_triage.reason: The full text directly addresses and tests the empirical objections in Easterlin’s reply with expanded national time series and additional survey data. Its reported trends conflict with the reply’s interpretation that happiness was flat or rising only in limited cases. The reference list identifies Easterlin’s 2005 reply. Supplied row 307 is Easterlin’s distinct 1974 paper, not this 2005 reply.
luna_triage.omission_quote:
With respect to Western Europe he points out that happiness has not risen in all countries
      and that the overall pattern shows little or no trend.
luna_triage.identity_quote:
Easterlin, R.A (2005)
Feeding the illusion of growth and happiness: A reply to Hagerty and Veenhoven
Social Indicators Research, vol. 74, pp.429-443
